commit_reviews.summary: Implements all Session 5 cross-cutting requirements (per-client rate limiting, paginated /history endpoint, background TTL cleanup) cleanly within the existing MessageStore/NotificationServer/HTTP-handler structure, with proper task cancellation and lock usage.

compounding_issues: Tracked __pycache__/*.pyc binary artifacts are committed in every session, polluting diffs and inflating each commit's noise (agent even notes it).
Session 1 greenfield discarded the entire 260-line seed, so the initial seed provided no architectural anchor and everything restarted on a new design.
S3's Redis test hook uses RedisBackbone.__new__ plus manual field assignment in NotificationServer.__init__ to inject a fake client — a fragile testability hack that persists into S5.
S4 refactor was partial: only the WebSocket transport was extracted; MessageStore, RedisBackbone, and the HTTP server remain monolithic in app.py, limiting the pluggability benefit.
S2's handle_message contains duplicated `if channel is not None` routing logic and channel-vs-payload channel detection that never gets cleaned up.
key_decisions: Greenfield rewrite as a pure asyncio WebSocket server (threading.RLock client registry, module-level NotificationServer app) rather than building on the Flask seed.
Channel subscription model with in-memory channel registry and subscribe/unsubscribe message types, introspectable via HTTP /channels endpoints.
Redis pub/sub as the message backbone with a silent in-process fallback when Redis is absent, keeping single-node operation working.
SQLite MessageStore for persistence shared by HTTP and websocket paths, later indexed for history queries.
Pluggable BaseTransport abstraction extracted in S4, decoupling routing from the WebSocket protocol.
Redis-backed fixed-window per-client rate limiting and a background hourly TTL cleanup loop in S5.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically. The codebase grew from 181 to 582 lines and 3 to 8 passing tests with zero test failures or error exits across all five sessions, while cost stayed flat and low ($0.012–$0.018/run). The arc is textbook: S1 established a clean greenfield architecture, S2 layered features without breakage, S3 made the largest architectural jump (Redis backbone + persistence, depth 15) yet kept tests green, S4 refactored for pluggability without regressing behavior, and S5 capped it with production-grade cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, indexed history, TTL cleanup). Later sessions built directly on prior interfaces (transport, store, backbone) rather than reworking them, and each commit left the suite green.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, steadily improving 5-session build where each layer (core server → channels → Redis backbone → pluggable transport → cross-cutting hardening) stacked cleanly on the last, marred only by minor hygiene issues like committed .pyc files and a partial refactor.
